A typed key — an integer, a string, a float — gets converted once into a fixed, byte-comparable form, so every comparison anywhere in the tree is a plain byte-for-byte check, never a type-aware parse.
Fill leaf pages left to right, keep the growing root only in memory, and only ever split the single page furthest to the right — because a sorted build never comes back to a page that's already full.
Fill factor is the percentage a page is packed to on a build or a right-edge append. Packing it completely full wastes nothing today, but risks a flood of splits on the very next write.

items.item: Fill factor is a genuine trade-off, not a tuning mistake to avoid — the right value depends on whether the table is static or still taking writes, which is exactly why PostgreSQL exposes it as a parameter rather than hard-coding one value.

items.item: Lazy, split-time-only deduplication is cheaper than any background sweep specifically because most pages never split at all — a sweep would spend I/O on pages a lazy scheme never touches.

items.item: A slot array's offsets, not the tuples themselves, are what stay sorted and contiguous — the actual key-value bytes can sit anywhere in the growing data area, which is exactly what lets a new tuple claim free space without disturbing any tuple already placed.

items.item: PostgreSQL's choice not to compress deduplication's posting lists is a concurrency trade-off, not an oversight — compressed lists would make deleting one row's pointer out of a shared posting list far more expensive under concurrent access.
